title: Kathina again

lines: THEY HAD NOTHING TO BATHE IN.
cards: A heavy rain is falling on the city of Savatthi. A servant girl runs to the monastery with a message: the meal is ready, the monks are invited. She comes back puzzled.
There are no monks there, she says, only naked ascetics standing out in the rain. Her mistress, a wealthy laywoman named Visakha, understands at once.
The monks had taken off their robes to bathe in the rain, because they had no other cloth to bathe in. They're monks, she tells the girl. Go back.
The rains retreat ends in gifts, and Kathina is its robe offering. You've met it before. Today, meet the woman in the monastic rule who taught the community what a useful gift looks like.

teach.b: After the meal, the rule says, Visakha asks the Buddha for a favor. He answers that awakened ones don't grant favors blindly.

So she names what she wants: to give, for as long as she lives, cloth for monks to bathe in during the rains. Food for monks arriving in town who don't know where to go for alms. Food for monks setting out on a journey.
Food and medicine for the sick, and food for the ones nursing them. Rice gruel in the mornings. And bathing cloth for the nuns.
Then the Buddha asks her why.
What good does she see in each one? She answers each, plainly. The new arrival, tired and lost, can eat and then go looking.
The nurse doesn't have to leave the sick monk to fetch food.
Every item comes from paying attention to someone's real need. The Buddha grants her request and praises her giving. Now the line to Kathina.

At the end of the rains, after months in one place, robes are worn thin. Lay people bring new cloth, and the community gives it to one monk to make a robe that day. It's a gift that fits the moment, just as Visakha's did.
The Dhammapada says, in Max Müller's words, "let him overcome the greedy by liberality." Visakha's way of being liberal wasn't a grand gesture. It was noticing who was standing in the rain.

how: In Theravada countries, in the month after the rains retreat, lay people bring robe cloth and other useful gifts to a monastery in a Kathina ceremony, and the community gives the cloth to one monk to make into a robe.

o: the robe offering at the rains' end, cloth for one monk's robe
a vow monks take to wear one robe for the whole year
the first meal lay people offer monks as the rains begin

p: they don't know where to go
no need to leave the sick
made into a robe for one monk

s: the servant girl found the monks bathing naked in the rain
she thought they were naked ascetics. they had no cloth to bathe in.
the Buddha granted Visakha's favor before hearing it

games.q: you're Visakha. your servant comes back saying there are no monks at the monastery, only naked ascetics in the rain. what do you do?
o: realize they're bathing, send her back, and later ask to give bathing cloth.
games.why: she understood at once, sent the girl back, and then asked the Buddha to let her give cloth for bathing in the rains.

practice: Look around your own circle the way Visakha did: who is standing in the rain in some small way, a coworker new to town, a neighbor caring for a sick parent, a student far from home?
Let one person come to mind and ask her question: not what would look generous, but what would actually help, a meal, a lift, an umbrella, literally. Choose one, then rest with the breath.

wordCard.voice: Kathina. The robe offering at the end of the rains, when lay people bring cloth and the community makes a robe for one monk. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali kathina: the name of the robe-cloth ceremony at the end of the rains.

carryVoice: Your line: the rains end in gifts. The useful gift is the one that fits the need. See you after the rain.
